A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same expert-neuron representation study. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison despite the changed title. V3 contains unresolved citations and cross-references, but the corresponding substantive content can generally be identified.

before.justification: V2 reports original expert-discovery experiments, MEN and SPP alignment results, domain-organization analyses and investigations across model sizes and training checkpoints.

after.justification: V3 retains those original empirical results and adds activation-steering experiments, Gemma evaluations and further analyses of expert representations.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains AP-based neuron identification, expertise thresholding and Jaccard comparison of expert sets. ExpertLens names the retained approach. V3's top-500 activation clamping is used in an added causal-validation experiment; it does not replace the representation-extraction procedure.

E1.justification: MEN, SPP and the manually curated semantic domains remain. V3 adds a focused neutral-prompt generation task assessing whether steering increases concept-related vocabulary. It removes v2 Appendix G's auxiliary Pythia benchmark coverage, including PIQA, MMLU and LogiQA. The Gemma addition changes evaluated models rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V2 compares against single-word embeddings from the input and final layers. V3 retains the input-layer comparator but replaces final-layer single-word embeddings with averaged contextualized sentence embeddings. Appendix B also introduces an unmodified Pythia-1b control for the steering experiment; randomized-domain controls remain.

E3.justification: V3 introduces controlled generation with zero versus 500 activated experts, 5,000 generated sentences per condition, temperature 1.0, a 300-token limit and exclusion of probing-set vocabulary. It also evaluates pretrained versus instruction-tuned Gemma-2b and adds symmetrized KL divergence as a similarity-analysis alternative. Appendix B inconsistently describes fifty concepts but reports outcomes for sixty.

E4.justification: V3 adds causal steering validation with unseen-word filtering and generation examples, an instruction-tuning analysis, KL-divergence comparisons and shared-versus-unshared expert AP histograms. Layer analyses expand to intermediate expertise thresholds, while v2's separate MLP and attention subcomponent analyses are removed. Broader-versus-narrower concept analyses are retained and regrouped.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix B introduces a two-sided permutation test for the steering effect. The existing eight-fold pilot procedure, bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals and SPP mixed-effects analysis remain. Additional figures using the same confidence-interval practice do not establish additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: V3 adds sentence-embedding results, Gemma results showing no significant instruction-tuning difference, KL correlations and AP histograms. Appendix B reports a 0.181% increase in previously unseen related-word prevalence after steering. The MEN correlations of 0.70, 0.77 and 0.79 and Table 2 remain unchanged; v2's final-layer single-word results and auxiliary benchmark accuracy summary are removed.

T1.justification: The concept, activation and expertise definitions remain substantively unchanged. Neither version develops theorems or proofs. V3's standard symmetrized KL expression accompanies an empirical metric comparison rather than a new mathematical derivation or formal result.

C1.justification: The central claims of stable expert representations, near-human alignment and human-like domain organization remain. V3 extends the embedding-superiority claim to sentence embeddings and explicitly presents ExpertLens as a lightweight tool for interpretability at scale. Much of the changed emphasis is reframing of contributions already present in v2.

C2.justification: V3 qualifies the deeper-layer semantic-processing interpretation through threshold-dependent expert locations and possible surface-versus-semantic distinctions. It adds a substantive argument about human-interpretable polysemanticity and discusses safety alignment and synthetic-data applications. V2's caution about interpreting interventions on shared expert intersections disappears, although the new experiment activates individual concepts' experts.

D1.justification: V3 documents activation clamping, generation parameters, spaCy preprocessing and GPT-4-derived related-word filtering for the new experiment. It adds SPP permission and Gemma licensing information. Conversely, v2's temporal max-pooling instruction and explicit 1,000-pair MEN test count are omitted; the hardware and extraction-time disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion shifts substantially from representational alignment to mechanistic interpretability and activation steering. V3 adds coverage of probes, logit lenses, sparse autoencoders, patching and causal mediation, with new bibliography entries such as Belrose et al., Cunningham et al. and Goldowsky-Dill et al. Much of v2's alignment literature discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, conclusion and limitations undergo substantial rewriting around ExpertLens, with renamed sections and reorganized appendices. V3 also replaces working citations and internal references throughout the document with unresolved question marks, impairing attribution and navigation.

P2.justification: Figure 3 becomes a three-panel expert/sentence/word comparison, new analyses receive figures, and the former main-text layer figure moves into consolidated appendix displays. Layer plots are reorganized into five-threshold panels, broader/narrower plots are paired, and Table 2 receives expanded headings. Several formerly full-width appendix figures become smaller column-width displays.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens the evidence through a more informative contextualized embedding comparison, direct steering validation and Gemma checks. However, pervasive unresolved citations and cross-references materially reduce traceability, while Appendix B's fifty-versus-sixty concept inconsistency leaves the new intervention design ambiguous. These substantive gains and reporting problems prevent a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
